title: Squared-Squares
summary: Kaggle’s Squares in Squares competition: for every n from 1 to 1000, fit n unit squares into the smallest possible square. Scoring tools, a certified per-n merge pipeline and my own packing searches.
body: Squares in Squares is a Kaggle packing competition built on a classic open problem. For every n from 1 to 1000, place n unit squares, at any position and rotation with no overlaps, inside the smallest axis-aligned square you can. The score sums Ln/√n − 1 over every n, so a perfect packing scores zero and every single configuration counts. For most n the best packing is unknown, and the best known ones tend to use oddly tilted squares.

This repo is my toolkit and submission history. It reimplements the official metric, including the interval-arithmetic check that certifies tilted squares really are disjoint. It parses a public records page of packing diagrams into coordinates, and merges candidate files from public notebooks and my own searches one n at a time, keeping a change only when it is certified valid and strictly better. My own contributions include a fault-line dynamic program and an LP “snap” that tightens near-feasible layouts.
The submission started at the 28.94 score of a plain grid and now sits at about 22.26.
highlights: A local scorer that reproduces the official metric, with float64 screening and certified recheck of close pairs at 60 digits
A parser that turns the records page’s compact SVG diagrams into unit-square coordinates
Per-n certified merges, so the best submission never regresses
Fault-line DP and LP-snap searches for tilted packings

title: Shrimple
summary: A tiny pixel-art shrimp that lives in your Windows system tray and reminds you to sit up straight. No sounds, no pop-ups, just a shrimp.
body: Shrimple puts a 16×16 shrimp in its own little patch of sea in your system tray. When it’s time to check your posture, the shrimp starts slouching, probably the way you are. Ignore it and it curls up, the seaweed wilts, and eventually the water boils orange and the shrimp turns furious and hops in place. Sit up, click it, and it calms down and starts the countdown again.

Reminders are every 5 minutes to 1½ hours from the right-click menu. The timer resets on its own when you’ve clearly stepped away: after 5 minutes without input, on unlock, and on wake from sleep. It ships as a single shrimple.exe, built and released by GitHub Actions on every version tag.
highlights: All the pixel art is ASCII in the source, drawn into the tray icon at runtime
Seven moods, from calm to furious, driven by how long you’ve ignored it
Native Win32 tray icon, menu and timer, with settings in the registry
A preview example renders every mood on light and dark taskbars on any OS

title: Bridge-Crossing RL Sim
summary: Hierarchical reinforcement learning in a grid world. A manager agent picks sub-goals, a worker agent walks there, and together they learn to fetch a log, build a bridge and get home. A “profit-sharing” reward keeps their goals aligned.
body: A Django web app for watching a hierarchical reinforcement learning agent learn in real time. The agent lives in a grid world split by a river. To get home it has to pick up a bridge piece, place it in the river, cross, and walk to the house.

The work is split between two agents. The manager only sees the big picture (do I have the bridge piece, is it placed, have I crossed?) and issues sub-goals like GOTO_LOG or GOTO_RIVER. The worker sees its own position and moves up, down, left and right to reach whatever sub-goal it was handed.

Training two separate value estimators toward one shared goal is fragile. A few clumsy worker moves can drag the manager’s Q-values far from a strategy it had already found. The fix here is profit sharing, in the spirit of potential-based reward shaping: the manager is rewarded when a command actually changes the world (it said GOTO_LOG, and now the agent HAS_LOG), and the worker earns a cut of that profit every step, positive or negative depending on what the manager currently expects. That small signal is enough to tell the worker why a square is worth walking to.
highlights: Both agents are Q-learners backed by small neural networks, with periodically synced target networks to keep training stable
Hindsight Experience Replay lets the worker learn from failed attempts by relabeling them as successes toward wherever it actually ended up
Dense worker rewards: +100 for each milestone, −1000 for drowning, and a small penalty for every step
A Web Worker polls the simulation API so training runs without freezing the page, and you can inspect the worker’s live Q-value map

title: Vixxing
summary: Caller verification for IT help desks. Before anyone resets a password or MFA, the caller reads a live 6-digit TOTP code off their phone. Facts leak. Possession doesn’t.
body: Most account-takeover defenses assume the attack comes through a login screen. The help desk is a different door, and usually a weaker one. An attacker looks up an employee, calls in sounding legitimate (“I got a new phone and I’m locked out”), and talks an agent into resetting MFA. Every check the agent can run, from caller ID to employee ID to date of birth, only proves the caller knows facts. Facts leak.

Vixxing puts a possession factor on the phone call itself. Every employee enrolls a TOTP secret, the same RFC 6238 one-time-password standard their authenticator app already uses for login. When they call, the agent asks for the current 6-digit code, types it in, and gets a green Caller Verified or a red Do not proceed. Someone without the enrolled phone can’t pass, no matter how much they know about the person they’re pretending to be.
The name is a nod to the problem: vishing, or voice phishing.
highlights: One staff-facing dashboard to add employees, verify callers, search, and import or export CSV
Enrollment by email: the server generates a secret, renders it as a QR code and sends it through Microsoft Graph
Works with Microsoft Authenticator, Google Authenticator and any other TOTP app
Accepts the current 30-second window plus one on either side to allow for clock drift

title: ClaimTracker
summary: A Django rebuild of a legacy healthcare claims viewer. Reads EDI 837 claims and renders print-accurate UB-04 and CMS-1500 forms, with PDF, Word and CSV export.
body: A replacement for an aging internal claims viewer that nobody had documentation for. Healthcare claims arrive as X12 EDI 837 files, both institutional (837I) and professional (837P), and get parsed into a SQL Server database. ClaimTracker reads them back out and shows each claim the way people actually know it: as a UB-04 or CMS-1500 form.

The forms are print-accurate, down to the real numbered-box layout. Staff can browse by date, provider or member, or search directly, see the claim’s live adjudication status, and export the open claim as a PDF, a Word document or a CSV.
Most of the work was reading the old system closely enough to reproduce what it actually did, not what anyone remembered it doing.
highlights: Feature parity with the legacy viewer: search, browse and the real form layouts
Live adjudication status for the selected claim
PDF, Word (.docx) and CSV export from a floating export button
Access control with an audit trail of who viewed which claim

title: Window-Works
summary: An interactive office floor plan. Look up your seat, reserve a free desk, and let admins repaint the layout without touching the database.
body: The office floor plan used to live in a spreadsheet. Window-Works turns it into an interactive map with color-coded departments, badges for free, occupied and kiosk desks, and a detail view for every seat showing who sits there and any notes.

Staff type their name to find their current desk, with no account or approval needed, and can claim any free desk, which automatically ends their previous assignment for the day. Admins get a visual layout editor: select a group of cells, assign a department, override colors or notes, and record temporary or permanent desk and work-from-home assignments.
highlights: Right-click panning and accessible color contrast on every desk
A live banner showing your current assignment and how long you’ve had it
An admin dashboard of active assignments with one-click end
SQLite and WhiteNoise, so it runs almost anywhere

title: Employee Directory
summary: A company directory built over a legacy Microsoft Access database, sorted by department and hierarchy, with birthdays and work anniversaries on the front page.
body: An internal employee directory built on top of a legacy Microsoft Access database, which kept working the whole time. Employees are grouped by department and ordered by the real reporting hierarchy, and department heads and supervisors get a watermark on their cards.

The homepage celebrates everyone with a birthday or work anniversary this month, with extra emphasis on today’s. An advanced search filters by department, title, hire date and supervisor status, and any set of results exports to CSV.
highlights: Management commands to parse and import employee records from the legacy database
Syncs company events from SharePoint
Custom themes and a lightweight analytics middleware
A demo seed command, so the public version runs without real employee data

title: Normalization Sim
summary: An agent-based toy model of what happens when AI pulls everyone’s opinions toward the mean. Tracks stability, Gini inequality, opinion diversity and trust over time.
body: What happens to a society when an AI quietly nudges everyone’s opinions toward the average? What if it does the opposite and amplifies the extremes for engagement? This simulation is a hackable toy for poking at those questions, built to be visual enough for a Primer-style explainer.

Agents are split into a majority and a minority with unequal starting resources, and “outlier” movements push on altruism, trust, polarization and policy. One dial, lambda, sets how hard opinions are pulled toward the mean, and engagement mode flips it to push them apart instead. Every simulated day it records stability, inequality (Gini), opinion and affiliation diversity, average trust, and how many minority agents starve.
It’s a teaching toy, not a prediction engine: something for building intuition about tradeoffs.
highlights: Command-line dials for population, days, normalization strength and minority share
CSV metrics, matplotlib plots and an optional GIF of the agents over time

title: Sprite-Mapper
summary: Upload a sprite sheet, click a tile, get its coordinates. No more counting rows and columns by hand.
body: A tiny single-page tool for anyone who has squinted at a sprite sheet counting tiles. Upload the sheet, enter the tile size and any margin between tiles, and click: you get the tile’s x and y coordinates instantly, with the selected tile outlined in red.
It’s one HTML file. No install, no build step.

title: Fruit Classifier
summary: A single-neuron network in pure NumPy that tells limes from lemons by weight and color. Sigmoid, backprop and gradient descent, all by hand.
body: Written in high school, back when OpenAI was still focused on Gym, to understand neural networks without anyone else’s library doing the thinking. It’s one neuron with two inputs, a fruit’s weight and its color (0 for green, 1 for yellow), and one output: lime or lemon.

Everything is done by hand: random weight initialization, a sigmoid forward pass, backpropagation through the sigmoid’s derivative, and gradient descent over 10,000 iterations. From the same era: a from-scratch linear regression that demonstrates gradient descent, and a reworked version of Karpathy’s min-char-rnn.
